summary.text: Titan is the largest moon of Saturn and the second largest moon in the Solar System.
It is the only moon known to have a dense atmosphere, and the only known object besides Earth with clear evidence of stable bodies of surface liquid.
Its methane cycle nearly resembles Earth's water cycle at a much lower temperature, so it is sometimes called the most Earth-like object in the Solar System.

facts.label: Lakes
facts.value: Cassini found liquid hydrocarbon lakes in its polar regions

items.prompt: Titan is wider than Mercury yet has much less mass. Why?

options.label: It is mostly ice, while Mercury is mostly iron and rock
Much of its width is thick gas rather than solid
It is hollow beneath a thin outer shell of rock
Saturn's gravity keeps pulling mass away from it

items.explain: Mercury is mainly iron and rock while Titan is mostly ice, which is less dense.

items.prompt: Titan has rivers, lakes and seas, like Earth. What are they most likely made of?

options.label: Plain liquid water, as in Earth's oceans
Probably liquid methane and ethane
Molten rock that cooled into smooth shapes
Liquid nitrogen pooled from the air

items.explain: Titan's seas are probably liquid methane and ethane, and its climate is far colder than Earth's.

items.prompt: Spacecraft only began to learn what Titan's surface looks like when Cassini–Huygens arrived in 2004. What had hidden it?

options.label: Saturn's rings, which sit between it and us
Thick dust storms that swept its surface
A dense, opaque atmosphere wrapped around it
Its small size, too tiny to see in detail

items.explain: The dense opaque atmosphere blocked understanding of Titan's surface until Cassini–Huygens.

items.prompt: On Earth, water evaporates, falls as rain and fills lakes. What is the closest match on Titan?

options.label: A rock cycle driven by moving crustal plates
A nitrogen cycle fed by steam from volcanoes
An ice cycle where glaciers melt each summer
A methane cycle through its air and surface liquids

items.explain: Titan's liquids and nitrogen atmosphere support a methane cycle that nearly resembles Earth's water cycle.

items.prompt: Hyperion sits in a stable orbit near Titan. What happened to other bodies that made close approaches to Titan?

options.label: They were pulled into tight orbits as new moons
Titan, being so massive, absorbed or ejected them
They skimmed its atmosphere and carried on past
They settled into the same stable island as Hyperion

items.explain: Hyperion probably formed in a stable orbital island, while the massive Titan absorbed or ejected any other bodies that came close.

items.prompt: A day on Titan lasts exactly as long as its trip around Saturn. What follows from that?

options.label: Saturn rises and sets in Titan's sky each day
Titan shows each of its sides to Saturn in turn
Titan permanently shows just one face to Saturn
Titan speeds up its spin as it nears Saturn

items.explain: Titan is tidally locked, so its rotation period equals its orbital period and one face always looks at Saturn.

paragraphs.heading: Saturn's giant moon
paragraphs.text: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and second only to Jupiter's Ganymede among all moons in the Solar System. It is 5,149.53 km across, bigger than the planet Mercury. Yet it has only 40% of Mercury's mass, because Mercury is mostly iron and rock while Titan is mostly ice, which is less dense. Compared with Earth's Moon, Titan is about 48% wider and 80% more massive.

paragraphs.heading: A thick sky and liquid seas
paragraphs.text: Titan is the only moon known to have a dense atmosphere, one thicker than Earth's. It is also the only known place besides Earth with clear evidence of stable liquid on its surface. The air is mostly nitrogen and methane, and smaller ingredients form hydrocarbon clouds and a heavy haze.

paragraphs.heading: Weather like Earth's
paragraphs.text: Titan has wind and rain, and its climate carves dunes, rivers, lakes, seas and deltas much like those on Earth, with seasonal weather patterns. The seas are probably liquid methane and ethane. Methane moves through a cycle that works much like Earth's water cycle, but at about 94 K (−179 °C). For these reasons Titan is sometimes called the most Earth-like body in the Solar System.

paragraphs.heading: Inside and on the surface
paragraphs.text: Titan is made mostly of ice and rock: a rocky core wrapped in layers of ice, including an icy crust and a buried layer of liquid water rich in ammonia. Its surface is young in geological terms and mostly smooth, with few impact craters, though mountains and several possible cryovolcanoes have been found. The thick, opaque air hid that surface until the Cassini–Huygens mission arrived in 2004. That mission found lakes of liquid hydrocarbons near the poles and discovered that the atmosphere super-rotates.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery and naming
paragraphs.text: Christiaan Huygens found Titan on March 25, 1655, with a telescope he built with help from his elder brother Constantijn. It was the first known moon of Saturn. Huygens called it Saturni Luna, Latin for "moon of Saturn". The name Titan came from John Herschel in 1847, after the Titans, the gods who came before the Olympians in Greek myth. The IAU officially numbers it Saturn VI.

paragraphs.heading: Orbit and day
paragraphs.text: Titan circles Saturn about 1.2 million km above its visible surface, once every 15 days and 22 hours. It is tidally locked, always showing Saturn the same face, so its day is exactly as long as its orbit. Seen from Titan, Saturn without its rings would look more than ten times as large as the Moon looks from Earth. The small, irregular moon Hyperion is in a 3:4 resonance with Titan, going around three times for every four Titan orbits.

paragraphs.heading: A violent beginning
paragraphs.text: The regular moons of Jupiter and Saturn probably grew from disks of material around the young planets. Titan, though, towers over the rest of Saturn's system, and its orbit has a high eccentricity that this process alone does not readily explain. One model says Saturn first had moons like Jupiter's Galilean moons, until giant impacts broke them up and built Titan. Mid-sized moons such as Rhea and Iapetus would have formed from the debris, and such a violent start would explain Titan's eccentric orbit.
